questions.a: A cross-encoder scores query and document together for the top candidates, improving precision over bi-encoder similarity.

questions.q: How do you chunk documents?
questions.a: Structure-aware or semantic splits with modest overlap, retaining metadata, with parent-child retrieval or contextual summaries where chunks lose meaning alone.

questions.q: How do you evaluate an LLM application?
questions.a: Build a labelled set of realistic cases, grade with code, rubrics and calibrated LLM judges, check retrieval separately, run in CI and monitor online metrics.

questions.q: Name biases of LLM-as-judge.
questions.a: Preference for longer answers, for the first position and for its own style; mitigate with pairwise swaps, rubrics and calibration against human labels.

questions.q: Design an agent loop and its safeguards.
questions.a: Plan, call tools, observe, repeat with a step and cost budget, timeouts, validated tool arguments, human approval for risky actions, idempotent tools and full tracing.

questions.q: What is Graph RAG?
questions.a: Building a knowledge graph of entities and relations from documents to retrieve connected context or community summaries, helping multi-hop and corpus-wide questions.

questions.q: How do you cut LLM cost and latency?
questions.a: Prompt caching of stable prefixes, model routing and distillation, shorter prompts and outputs, batching, semantic caching, streaming and parallel tool calls.

questions.q: How do you version and release prompt changes?
questions.a: Treat prompts as code: store in version control, test against the evaluation set, canary or A/B release, pin model versions and keep rollback ready.

questions.q: Long context or retrieval?
questions.a: Long context is simple but costly and can lose information in the middle; retrieval scales to large corpora and is cheaper, but needs good indexing. Combine them: retrieve then place a concise context.

questions.q: Why can't you shuffle time series data for train-test splits?
questions.a: The future would leak into training, giving unrealistically good results. Split by time and evaluate on later data.

questions.q: What are the components of a time series?
questions.a: Trend, seasonality, cycles and noise (remainder), combined additively or multiplicatively.

questions.q: What is stationarity and how do you achieve it?
questions.a: Constant mean, variance and autocorrelation over time. Difference to remove trend, seasonally difference to remove seasonality and take logs to stabilise variance.

questions.q: What baselines should a forecast beat?
questions.a: Naive (last value) and seasonal naive (value one season ago); a complex model that cannot beat them is not worth deploying.

questions.q: Explain exponential smoothing.
questions.a: A weighted average of past observations with geometrically decaying weights: level = alpha x observation + (1 - alpha) x previous level; Holt and Holt-Winters add trend and seasonality.

questions.q: What is ARIMA(p, d, q)?
questions.a: Autoregression on p lags, d differences to achieve stationarity and a moving average of q past errors; SARIMA adds seasonal terms.

questions.q: What does the ACF show?
questions.a: Correlation of the series with lagged copies of itself: peaks reveal seasonality and slow decay indicates non-stationarity; the PACF shows direct lag effects.

questions.q: Explain walk-forward validation.
questions.a: Train on data up to an origin, forecast the next horizon, score, then move the origin forward and repeat, averaging errors, which mimics real deployment.

questions.q: Why is MAPE problematic?
questions.a: It explodes or is undefined near zero actuals and penalises over-forecasts and under-forecasts asymmetrically; MASE or MAE are safer.

questions.q: How do you use gradient boosting for forecasting?
questions.a: Create lag, rolling and calendar features using only past information, train a global model across series, and forecast directly per horizon or recursively.

questions.q: Direct versus recursive multi-step forecasting?
questions.a: Direct trains one model per horizon; recursive reuses a one-step model feeding back forecasts, which compounds errors but is simpler.

questions.q: How would you detect anomalies in seasonal data?
questions.a: Compare against a seasonal baseline (same time in previous cycles) or a forecast, using robust statistics such as MAD on the residuals, then tune thresholds and minimum duration to limit false alerts.

questions.q: What is a prediction interval and why report it?
questions.a: A range expected to contain the future value with stated probability; decisions such as safety stock depend on the upper quantile, not the mean.

questions.q: How do you forecast intermittent demand?
questions.a: Specialised methods such as Croston or probabilistic count models, evaluated with quantile or inventory-based metrics rather than MAPE.

questions.q: MLE versus MAP versus Bayesian inference?
questions.a: MLE maximises the likelihood, MAP adds a prior and takes the posterior mode, and Bayesian inference keeps the entire posterior distribution.

questions.q: State Bayes' rule in words.
questions.a: The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior, normalised by the evidence.

questions.q: What is a conjugate prior? Give an example.
questions.a: A prior for which the posterior has the same functional form, such as a Beta prior with a Bernoulli likelihood giving Beta(a + heads, b + tails).

questions.q: Credible versus confidence interval?
questions.a: A credible interval contains the parameter with a stated posterior probability given the model and prior; a confidence interval is a procedure that covers the truth in a stated fraction of repeated experiments.

questions.q: What does L2 regularisation correspond to in Bayesian terms?
questions.a: A zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights; L1 corresponds to a Laplace prior.

questions.q: Explain Thompson sampling.
questions.a: Sample a success rate from each option's posterior and play the option with the largest sample, balancing exploration and exploitation.

questions.q: How does Metropolis-Hastings work?
questions.a: Propose a nearby point and accept it with probability min(1, p(new)/p(old)); after burn-in the visited points are samples from the target distribution.

questions.q: How do you diagnose MCMC convergence?
questions.a: Run several chains from different starts, compare them with R-hat near 1, inspect trace plots and check the effective sample size.

questions.q: What is a Gaussian process and what does it give you?
questions.a: A prior over functions defined by a kernel; conditioning on data yields predictions with calibrated uncertainty that grows away from observations. Cost is O(n^3).

questions.q: Explain the EM algorithm.
questions.a: For latent-variable models: the E-step computes posterior responsibilities of the latent variables given current parameters; the M-step maximises the expected complete-data likelihood. Likelihood never decreases.

questions.q: Aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty?
questions.a: Aleatoric is irreducible noise in the data; epistemic is lack of knowledge about the model and can shrink with more data.

questions.q: How do deep ensembles and MC dropout estimate uncertainty?
questions.a: Disagreement between independently trained networks, or between stochastic forward passes with dropout enabled, approximates epistemic uncertainty.

questions.q: Explain conformal prediction.
questions.a: Use a calibration set's residual quantile to build intervals around any model's predictions, guaranteeing coverage under exchangeability.

questions.q: What is calibration and how do you fix miscalibration?
questions.a: Predicted probabilities matching observed frequencies. Measure with reliability diagrams and ECE; fix with temperature scaling, Platt scaling or isotonic regression on validation data.

questions.q: What tasks does graph machine learning cover?
questions.a: Node classification, link prediction, graph classification or regression, community detection, ranking and graph generation.

questions.q: What is PageRank?
questions.a: The stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with probability d and jumps to a random node otherwise, computed by power iteration.

questions.q: What is homophily and why does it matter?
questions.a: Connected nodes tend to share labels or features, so aggregating neighbour information helps; on heterophilous graphs plain message passing can hurt.

questions.q: Explain one layer of a graph neural network.
questions.a: Each node aggregates its neighbours' features with a permutation-invariant function and combines the result with its own features through learned weights and a nonlinearity.

questions.q: GCN versus GraphSAGE versus GAT?
questions.a: GCN uses degree-normalised averaging, GraphSAGE samples neighbours and supports inductive learning at scale, GAT learns attention weights over neighbours.

questions.q: What is over-smoothing?
questions.a: With many layers node representations become nearly identical because repeated averaging mixes information across the graph; use few layers, residuals and normalisation.

questions.q: How does DeepWalk create node embeddings?
questions.a: Random walks generate node sequences that are treated as sentences for skip-gram training, so nodes co-occurring in walks get similar vectors.

questions.q: Common link prediction heuristics?
questions.a: Common neighbours, Jaccard similarity, Adamic-Adar and preferential attachment, evaluated with held-out edges and negative samples.

questions.q: What is over-squashing?
questions.a: Information from exponentially many distant nodes must pass through fixed-size vectors along narrow paths, limiting long-range dependencies.

questions.q: How do you train GNNs on a graph with billions of edges?
questions.a: Neighbour sampling (GraphSAGE), cluster or subgraph batching and distributed training; full-neighbourhood training is infeasible because the receptive field grows exponentially.

questions.q: What avoids leakage when evaluating link prediction?
questions.a: Remove test edges from the graph used for message passing, split by time where relevant and sample realistic negatives.

questions.q: What are knowledge graph embeddings (TransE)?
questions.a: Entities and relations are vectors trained so that head + relation is close to tail for true triples, enabling completion of missing facts.

questions.q: What is GraphRAG and when does it beat vector RAG?
questions.a: Retrieval over a graph of extracted entities and relations, useful for multi-hop questions and global summaries; costlier to build and maintain.

questions.q: When would you not use a GNN?
questions.a: When a tabular model with engineered graph features (degree, PageRank, neighbour statistics) already performs well, or the graph has low homophily or little structure.

questions.q: Why prefer an interpretable model when possible?
questions.a: Simple models can be audited, debugged and trusted more easily, and often perform nearly as well on tabular data.

questions.q: What is permutation importance?
questions.a: The drop in a held-out metric when one feature's values are shuffled, showing reliance on that feature; it can mislead with correlated features.

questions.q: Explain Shapley values for feature attribution.
questions.a: Each feature's average marginal contribution over all orders of adding features; they sum to the prediction minus the baseline and are computed exactly for small models or approximated (TreeSHAP, sampling).

questions.q: What is a counterfactual explanation?
questions.a: The smallest feasible change to the input that would change the decision, such as 'approved if income were 5,000 higher', ideally actionable and plausible.

questions.q: Define demographic parity, equal opportunity and equalised odds.
questions.a: Equal selection rates across groups; equal true positive rates; equal true and false positive rates.

questions.q: Why can't all fairness criteria hold at once?
questions.a: When base rates differ, calibration and equalised odds are mutually incompatible for imperfect classifiers, so choices reflect policy and context.

questions.q: Where does bias enter an ML system?
questions.a: In problem framing and labels, sampling and historical data, proxy features, optimisation of average metrics, thresholds, and deployment feedback loops.

questions.q: What is differential privacy?
questions.a: A guarantee that any one person's data changes the probability of any output by at most a factor e^epsilon, achieved by adding calibrated noise.

questions.q: What is membership inference?
questions.a: An attack that decides whether a record was in the training data by exploiting model confidence differences, a privacy risk for overfit models.

questions.q: What is an adversarial example and how does FGSM make one?
questions.a: An input with a small, targeted perturbation that changes the prediction; FGSM adds epsilon times the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input.

questions.q: How do you defend against adversarial attacks?
questions.a: Adversarial training, certified or randomised-smoothing defences, input validation, ensembles and monitoring, plus treating model outputs as untrusted in downstream systems.

questions.q: What belongs in a model card?
questions.a: Intended use and limits, training data, metrics by slice, ethical considerations, risks and maintenance contacts.

questions.q: How do you test for proxy discrimination?
questions.a: Check whether non-protected features predict the protected attribute, evaluate outcomes and error rates by group, and use counterfactual tests or feature ablations.

questions.q: What does DP-SGD do?
questions.a: It clips each example's gradient and adds Gaussian noise during training, with accounting that tracks the privacy budget spent.

questions.q: How many FLOPs does training a transformer need?
questions.a: About 6 x parameters x tokens: 2ND for the forward pass and 4ND for the backward pass.

questions.q: How much memory per parameter does mixed-precision Adam training need?
questions.a: About 16 bytes: 2 for bf16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for fp32 master weights and 8 for the two Adam moments, plus activations.

questions.q: Why bf16 instead of fp16 for training?
questions.a: bf16 has fp32's exponent range so it needs no loss scaling, while fp16's narrow range risks overflow and underflow.

questions.q: What is MFU?
questions.a: Model FLOPs utilisation: useful model FLOP/s divided by the hardware's peak FLOP/s; well-tuned runs reach about 35 to 55%.

questions.q: Explain activation checkpointing.
questions.a: Store only some activations and recompute the others in the backward pass, trading about 33% more compute for much less memory.

questions.q: Data parallel versus tensor parallel versus pipeline parallel?
questions.a: Data parallel splits the batch with full model copies; tensor parallel splits individual matrices; pipeline parallel splits layers into stages processed in micro-batches.

questions.q: What does ZeRO stage 3 / FSDP do?
questions.a: Shards optimiser state, gradients and parameters across data-parallel ranks so memory per GPU falls to about 16 psi / p, at the cost of gathering weights layer by layer.

questions.q: What is the pipeline bubble?
questions.a: Idle time of (p - 1)/(m + p - 1) with p stages and m micro-batches; reduced by more micro-batches or interleaved schedules.

questions.q: Why place tensor parallelism inside a node?
questions.a: It requires an all-reduce per layer and so needs NVLink-class bandwidth; inter-node links are too slow.

questions.q: Explain the roofline model.
questions.a: Attainable performance is min(peak FLOP/s, bandwidth x arithmetic intensity); low-intensity operations are memory bound and high-intensity ones compute bound.

questions.q: Why is decoding memory bound and how do you help it?
questions.a: Each generated token reads all the weights for few FLOPs. Batch more sequences, use quantisation, KV-cache optimisations, speculative decoding and fused kernels.

questions.q: What is FlashAttention?
questions.a: An exact attention algorithm that tiles computation in on-chip memory so the n x n score matrix never materialises in HBM, reducing memory traffic and memory use.

questions.q: State the Chinchilla result.
questions.a: For a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should scale together, about 20 tokens per parameter; many earlier models were under-trained.

questions.q: Why train a model beyond compute-optimal?
questions.a: Inference cost dominates over a model's lifetime, so a smaller model trained on more data reaches a quality target with cheaper serving.

questions.q: How do you handle failures in long training runs?
questions.a: Frequent asynchronous checkpoints including optimiser and data-loader state, automatic restart, health checks to evict bad nodes, and monitoring for loss spikes with rollback.

questions.q: Explain overfitting simply.
questions.a: The model memorises the training examples, including their noise, so it performs well on them and poorly on new data, like a student who memorised last year's answers.

questions.q: Explain gradient descent simply.
questions.a: Walk downhill on the loss by repeatedly stepping the parameters in the direction that reduces the error, with the learning rate setting the step size.

questions.q: Explain embeddings simply.
questions.a: A map where items with similar meaning are close together, so similarity search is finding nearby points.

questions.q: Explain precision and recall simply.
questions.a: Precision is how much of what you flagged is correct; recall is how much of the real positives you found.

questions.q: Explain attention simply.
questions.a: For each token, decide how much to listen to every other token and mix their information accordingly, with cost growing with the square of the length.

questions.q: Explain bias and variance simply.
questions.a: Bias is consistently missing the target because the model is too simple; variance is scattered answers because the model is too sensitive to the particular training data.

questions.q: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
questions.a: They are trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify facts, so they can fluently fill gaps with wrong information.

questions.q: Explain RAG simply.
questions.a: An open-book exam: retrieve relevant documents by meaning and put them in the prompt so the model answers from them.

questions.q: Explain LoRA simply.
questions.a: Freeze the base weights and train small low-rank add-on matrices, like sticky notes, so fine-tuning needs little memory and the adapters are small files.

questions.q: Explain quantisation simply.
questions.a: Store weights with fewer bits, like rounding prices, shrinking the model and speeding loading at a small accuracy cost.

questions.q: What does temperature do?
questions.a: It rescales the next-token probabilities: low temperature makes the model pick likely tokens, high temperature flattens the distribution for more varied output.

questions.q: Explain pre-training, fine-tuning and RLHF as an education.
questions.a: Pre-training is reading a vast library, supervised fine-tuning is apprenticeship from worked examples, preference tuning is a mentor's feedback on which answers are better.

questions.q: Why can accuracy be misleading?
questions.a: On imbalanced data a model that always predicts the majority class scores high accuracy while finding nothing; use precision, recall, PR curves or cost-based metrics.

questions.q: How would you explain a transformer to a manager?
questions.a: A stack of layers where every word looks at every other word to understand context, then thinks about it privately; processing everything in parallel makes it fast to train and powerful.
